opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it a bit carefully, because I don't think user feedback stops mattering. What's changing is where the signal for improving models actually comes from.

In the early phase, after pretraining on the internet, the big unlock was human feedback. You had people rating outputs, writing preferred responses, and that's how you turned a raw language model into something that behaves like an assistant. That worked well, but it has real limits. It's expensive, it's slow, and it's noisy. And as models get better, the average person often can't tell which of two answers is more correct, especially for complex code, math, or multi-step reasoning. People end up rewarding what sounds confident or pleasant rather than what's actually right. That's where a lot of the sycophancy problems came from.

So the shift is toward signals you can verify. If a model writes code, you can run it and see whether the tests pass. If it proves something, you can check the proof. If it's an agent doing a task, you can see whether the task got done. That kind of reinforcement learning from verifiable outcomes scales much better. You can generate huge amounts of it synthetically, and it doesn't plateau at the level of the human rater.

The other piece is that we're running out of fresh, high-quality human data. The labs have consumed most of the public internet, so more of the progress has to come from models generating their own data, testing it against some ground truth, and learning from that loop.

From my perspective, the concern is what gets lost. When the feedback loop is mostly the lab plus an automated verifier, the question of what the model should optimize for gets decided by a very small number of companies. That's part of why I care about user-owned AI. Users should still have a say in what these systems value and how they act on their behalf, even if the raw capability gains increasingly come from self-improvement and verification instead of thumbs-up and thumbs-down clicks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what we're seeing is that the leverage has shifted. Early on, user feedback was the main signal you had. You put a model in front of people, they clicked thumbs up or thumbs down, and that preference data fed back into RLHF and shaped the next version. That worked when models were mostly doing conversational tasks where human taste is the ground truth.

But a few things changed. First, human feedback is noisy, expensive, and increasingly out of its depth. If a model is writing a thousand lines of code or proving something in math, the average rater can't tell you if it's correct. They can tell you if it looks confident. That's a bad signal, and you end up optimizing for things that feel good rather than things that are right.

Second, the frontier of the work moved to domains with verifiable outcomes. Code either compiles and passes the tests or it doesn't. A math answer checks out or it doesn't. An agent either completes the task in the environment or fails. Once you have that, you don't need a human in the loop to tell you what good looks like. You can run reinforcement learning against the verifier directly, at a scale no amount of crowdsourced feedback could match. The models are effectively generating their own training signal.

And third, there's a data ownership issue underneath all of this that I care about a lot. User feedback flows into a closed system. People contribute, the company captures the value, and nobody outside gets to see what the model learned or why. So part of the shift is also a reaction to that. If the signal comes from open environments and verifiable tasks, it's at least reproducible by other people, and it opens the door to doing this in a more decentralized, user-owned way instead of everyone donating their preferences to one lab.

So I don't think user feedback disappears. It still matters for alignment, for tone, for the things that are inherently subjective. But it's no longer the engine of capability. The engine is now verifiable environments and the compute you can throw at them.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s less about moving away from user feedback and more about finding feedback you can scale. When a person rates an answer, that’s useful, but it’s expensive, and it’s often ambiguous. They may prefer an answer because it sounds convincing, even if it’s wrong.

With something like coding, you can run the code and see whether the tests pass. With math, you can sometimes verify the result. That gives the model a much clearer signal, and you can repeat that process many more times than you could with human reviewers.

But user feedback still matters, because passing a test doesn’t necessarily mean you solved the problem the user actually had. So I would frame this as a shift toward automated feedback for improving capabilities, while people still help define what those capabilities should accomplish.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure I would frame it as moving away from user feedback entirely. I think we’re moving toward training signals that are easier to verify. If a model writes code, you can run the tests. If it solves a math problem, you can check the answer. That gives you a much tighter feedback loop than asking somebody which of two responses they prefer.

User feedback is still important, because passing a test doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve built something useful. But collecting high-quality feedback from people is expensive, and preferences can be inconsistent. So there’s an incentive to automate the parts you can measure, while still using people to understand whether you’re solving the right problem.
